headline: Stocks are set to close a volatile, holiday-shortened week with an AI-led rebound, while Sanofi's $41 billion Insmed deal and Deutsche Boerse's cleared Allfunds takeover anchor a busy deals tape.

paragraphs.text: The biggest healthcare story is Sanofi's agreement to buy Insmed for $41 billion, per Fierce Pharma. The deal brings in three commercial and late-stage respiratory assets and is framed as a way to offset Dupixent's coming loss of exclusivity. Separately, Business Upturn notes that Sanofi shares reopened lower after an early drop following a recent rally. The list does not say the two items are linked, so treat any connection as unconfirmed. For dealmakers, the size confirms that large pharma is willing to pay up for late-stage growth rather than wait on internal pipelines.

paragraphs.text: Other transactions and financings were smaller. Fierce Biotech reports Bayer is the latest big drugmaker to turn to Hansoh Pharma for antibody-drug conjugate expertise, in a $3.3 billion deal for a phase 1 asset. That is a large headline number for such an early program. Bayer also faces a reimbursement dispute in Germany that is leading it to pull its kidney and heart failure drug Kerendia from the market there, according to Fierce Pharma. Schrödinger signed a €22 million all-cash biologics collaboration with Enpicom. On the private side, Marrow Therapeutics launched with $173 million for severe blood disorders, and Iambic Therapeutics, fresh off a $150 million IPO, released preclinical data on a possible CDK inhibitor challenger. Fierce also profiles Vyriad, a low-profile viral biotech with big-pharma partnerships. A Korean outlet says drug candidates developed in Korea are increasingly getting clinical-trial funding from overseas capital, and that founders should seek partners from Series A. Small buyouts in the list include Q-Line Biotech's $3 million purchase of a 70% stake in Heidelco Medicore, with little detail beyond that.

paragraphs.text: On the clinical and regulatory front, AbbVie's Rinvoq won FDA approval in nonsegmental vitiligo, the first oral therapy for the condition, setting up competition with Incyte's Opzelura. Cogent Biosciences won a second-line GIST approval, the first new option in about 20 years. Bristol Myers Squibb's Sotyktu had one win and one miss in two phase 3 lupus trials, which Fierce says leaves a mixed outlook for expansion. GSK is preparing filings for Exdensur in a rare vascular disease, about a year after its asthma approval. Smaller data points include positive phase 2 results from Desentum in birch pollen allergy and early DiaMedica data in fetal growth restriction. Lundbeck faces an epilepsy readout that MedWatch says could be a game changer, though the outcome is not yet known. Thermo Fisher received an expanded FDA clearance for its EXENT analyser. On the downside, the FDA sent noncompliance letters to two biotechs over trial-data reporting, Marksans Pharma received a six-observation Form 483, and Orca Bio is cutting an undisclosed number of jobs months after launching Tregzi.

paragraphs.text: Policy and payer news is dominated by cost pressure. CMS says its third round of Medicare negotiations cut prices on 13 Part B and Part D drugs, and that the lower prices would have saved about $9.2 billion, or 45%, had they applied in 2025. Ninety-five academic hospital executives asked Congress for a two-year delay to a CMS 340B reimbursement change that would cost 340B hospitals nearly $5.5 billion, with academic institutions bearing over half. Fewer ACA exchange choices are available in more regions per RWJF, a poll shows half of voters paying more in premiums and out-of-pocket costs, and WTW expects global health insurance costs to rise 10.2% next year. UnitedHealthcare's Surest has a new CEO focused on affordability. The Alliance for Regenerative Medicine's CEO describes a difficult year pushing back on the FDA's shifting gene therapy stance. Measles remains a public health concern, with Virginia's first death and Pennsylvania's ninth, and WSJ reports the Pennsylvania outbreak has hit Amish and Plain communities hardest. Montana's right-to-try law is drawing scrutiny over who bears cost and risk. Healthcare AI tie-ups continued, including Waystar with Google's Gemini and WebMD Ignite with ChatGPT.

paragraphs.text: US stocks look set to finish a wild, holiday-shortened week on a strong note. WSJ says Nasdaq futures were up about 2.7% ahead of the shortened Friday session, with the S&P 500 and Dow also higher. The NYT and FT both describe a week of violent swings as the AI trade, long dominant, gave way to a market struggling to price future earnings. Bloomberg says bulls are making a case for a short-term rebound. Not everyone is buying it. MarketWatch reports Goldman traders see about $100 billion of automated selling from trend-following funds still to come this year, JPMorgan's European quants think the AI stock crash is mostly over but warn of a worse phase in 2027, and one strategist is 100% in cash and calls buying the Nasdaq dip a falling knife. The market's mood has been tied to Nvidia. WSJ says President Trump engineered Jensen Huang's return to the chipmaker, and its columnists argue that a real bottom needs something more fundamental to change. Separately, NYT says Nvidia halted sales to four Southeast Asian countries after a new US rule requiring licenses for advanced chips.

paragraphs.text: Rates and commodities leaned toward higher yields and firmer risk appetite. Treasury yields rose in the shortened post-Thanksgiving session, and eurozone yields followed Treasuries and oil higher. Precious metals surged as investors returned to the AI trade and the liquidity-driven selling eased. Brent is above $97 a barrel on attacks on Gulf shipping and Saudi energy infrastructure, with the OPEC+ meeting this weekend in focus. Russia extended its jet fuel export ban through March as Ukraine continues to strike its refineries. Dubai's benchmark index erased its wartime losses and has gained nearly 14% this month. Higher energy prices and a new round of tariffs on 14 trading partners, per the FT, add to the inflation backdrop central banks are weighing.

paragraphs.text: Central banks are mostly leaning hawkish. The ECB's October account shows many officials saw another hike as necessary unless the inflation outlook improved significantly, and WSJ says the euro barely moved on news that Pablo Hernández de Cos is taking over, as Brown Brothers Harriman does not expect a near-term policy shift. The FT's Monetary Policy Radar says the Bank of England will defy market pricing and stick with gradual tightening. The Bank of Korea resumed hikes, and a BOJ board member urged timely increases, bolstering the case for a December move. In the US, WSJ argues the bar for the Fed to rescue markets has risen, and the FT says officials face a three-way tussle over inflation, AI and guidance.

paragraphs.text: Growth data is patchy. France's third-quarter GDP fell 0.2%, worse than first estimated, German consumer confidence ticked up from a subdued level, and Canadian payrolls rose in September after two declines. In China, the CSI 300 had its biggest one-day gain in two years after Beijing signalled more support. Industrial profit surged in October on strong tech exports, but the FT says households are shedding consumer debt as the mortgage decline spreads to consumer loans. In the US, NYT says consumers are trading off rather than cutting back. Market stress shows up elsewhere: Korea's pension fund lost about $151 billion of assets in the third quarter on the Kospi's retreat, Indonesia arrested three people over alleged market manipulation after MSCI threatened a downgrade, and Brazil's president named a banker as finance minister after an asset sell-off. Turkey's vice president said liquidated fund payouts will track market prices, so many small investors may not recover their principal.

paragraphs.text: Private credit coverage today is mostly skeptical or cautious, though the list gives only headlines and short blurbs. The FT's Markets desk argues that direct lending can be replicated in public markets, challenging the asset class's claim to a distinct alpha. Citywire says Pictet prefers infrastructure to private credit because taxes make it a no-go. New Private Markets reports Partners Capital is eyeing climate-related stress and sees credit managers diverging on ESG. Retail access is a recurring worry: one report says private market funds are testing retail investors with tight exit caps, a reminder that semi-liquid structures can strain when redemptions rise. Alternative Credit Investor says IMCO has named Fernando Martinez head of global credit. Pengana's listed private credit trust, PCX, is being promoted on its monthly payments.

FT Alphaville notes British and European banks have taken on a lot of France risk, which matters given the weak French GDP print and the political risk the FT attaches to Marine Le Pen's rise. The detail in the list is thin, so the scale of that exposure isn't clear.

paragraphs.text: In liquid credit, CNBC says fund managers advise being wary of rising correlations but taking high US credit yields. One hedge fund manager warned the AI boom could trigger a recession while still seeing data centers as attractive. Retail-oriented high-yield products are getting attention, including a newer high-yield bond ETF with reduced credit risk and volatility, and a municipal high-yield fund's third-quarter commentary, though these are not market-moving. Elsewhere, AGNC's 17.5% yield is drawing dividend-stock attention, and a Singapore piece warns of dividend traps. The common thread is investors chasing yield while the AI selloff and higher rates test credit appetite. Coverage of defaults and distress was light today.

paragraphs.text: The EU gave unconditional approval to Deutsche Boerse's €5.3 billion ($5.8 billion) acquisition of Allfunds, per Bloomberg, clearing the way for the largest acquisition in the exchange operator's history. Allfunds is also adding private markets capacity, with HarbourVest joining its private markets programme as part of a wealth push. In consumer staples, the WSJ reports Altria is exploring a deal for Imperial Brands, which has a market value of around $30 billion, and Bloomberg says the move could affect Altria's AB InBev stake as part of a possible three-way reshaping of the tobacco industry. Nothing in the list suggests a deal is agreed. Coca-Cola HBC completed its $2.6 billion acquisition of Coca-Cola Beverages Africa, and Thales said it plans to buy a 51.6% stake in laser maker Lumibird from its CEO and majority shareholder in a deal valued at $483 million, sending Lumibird shares sharply higher.

paragraphs.text: In private equity, EQT struck a deal for a majority stake in Apposite-backed Kelso Pharma, and TJC is buying a majority interest in healthcare events firm HMP Global with the aim of driving M&A. The FT reports Kirkland & Ellis is facing criticism from PE backers over continuation-vehicle contracts that, in the lawyers' view, remove investors' right to sue in a dispute. Continuation vehicles are a growing exit route for sponsors, so the governance question could affect how they are priced and marketed to LPs. Trump Media is also reportedly spending $8 million to $13 million plus expenses on proxy solicitation ahead of its merger vote.

paragraphs.text: The IPO pipeline is a mix of AI and regional listings. Gotrade reports Anthropic's stock has fallen 28% from its high and is back near its IPO price, and CNBC says it is teetering at a $1 trillion market cap as its post-IPO slide tests the AI trade. Inc. frames its $81 billion IPO as pointing to compute as the next big opportunity, and the WSJ says OpenAI's IPO countdown clock is ticking. The figures are as reported and are hard to reconcile from the list alone. Bloomberg says Fidelidade is preparing a Lisbon IPO from the second half of 2027, and India's Swara Baby Products set an 800 crore rupee IPO for December 2. The JSE is courting a secondary listing of Nigeria's Dangote refinery after its Nigerian IPO, and Hong Kong is offering sovereign wealth funds tax breaks after some global investors pulled out or scaled back teams. Binance is reportedly hiring Wall Street IPO specialists, which one crypto outlet reads as a sign of on-chain IPO plans, though that is speculation. Kalshi is eyeing microinsurance for small businesses to offset legal pressure on sports wagers.
